```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(disperseR)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +

```

# Why movement phases?

Dispersal links populations: it drives gene flow, the colonisation of empty
habitat and the persistence of metapopulations (Bowler & Benton 2005; Clobert
et al. 2012). GPS tracks of dispersing animals, however, mix several processes.
An individual may explore after leaving its natal area or after being released,
stop for a few hours or days on the way, settle temporarily, make excursions
and come back, or move between areas it already knows (Beier 1995; Zimmermann
et al. 2005). Each of these *movement phases* responds to different decisions
and takes place at a scale of days to weeks (Nathan et al. 2008; Getz 2022).

Separating them matters because animals use the landscape differently in each
phase. Habitat selection and the response to roads and human infrastructure
differ between resident and dispersing individuals, and even between types of
non-residential movement (Gastón et al. 2016; Cisneros-Araujo et al. 2025).
Connectivity models built from all locations together, or from all locations
outside home ranges, can therefore misrepresent how permeable the landscape is
for dispersers (Elliot et al. 2014). Short stops during long movements act as
stepping stones that make long-distance dispersal possible (Saura et al. 2014).
In reintroductions, the length of the exploratory phase after release and the
time until settlement are key indicators of success (Berger-Tal & Saltz 2014;
Cisneros-Araujo et al. 2026a).

Many methods segment tracks into behavioural units (Edelhoff et al. 2016;
Gurarie et al. 2016). Hidden Markov models (HMM) fitted to step lengths and
turning angles are among the most widely used (Morales et al. 2004; Langrock et
al. 2012; McClintock & Michelot 2018). At fine temporal resolution, however,
their states mostly describe *activity modes*, such as resting or moving, rather
than movement phases: a dispersing animal also rests every day, and a resident
one also moves within its home range (Getz 2022; Cisneros-Araujo et al. 2026b).
Identifying phases requires information on space use over longer periods, such
as residence time or spatial clustering (Barraquand & Benhamou 2008; Gastón et
al. 2016; Patin et al. 2020).

`disperseR` combines both scales. HMM states describe the activity of each
location. Density-based spatial clustering (DBSCAN; Ester et al. 1996; Hahsler
et al. 2019), together with minimum duration and activity criteria, identifies
**area-restricted phases** (ARP), such as home ranges, transient residences or
long stays. Short stops are not ARPs and remain part of the movement. Finally,
each movement between ARPs is classified according to the network of ARPs the
individual has visited so far.

## The classification

```{r scheme, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.2}
nodes <- data.frame(x = c(1.2, 4.6), y = c(1, 1.6), lab = c("ARP A", "ARP B"))
arrows <- data.frame(
  x = c(-0.6, 1.5, 4.9, 4.2), y = c(0.2, 1.15, 1.9, 1.35),
  xend = c(0.9, 4.25, 5.2, 1.55), yend = c(0.85, 1.6, 1.35, 0.95),
  phase = c("Type 0", "Type 2", "Type 1", "Type 3"),
  curv = c(0.2, -0.25, -1.6, -0.25))
p <- ggplot() + coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.8, 6.2), ylim = c(0, 2.6)) + theme_void()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(arrows))) {
  p <- p + geom_curve(data = arrows[i, ], aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = phase),
                      curvature = arrows$curv[i], linewidth = 1,
                      arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "inches"), type = "closed"))
}
p + geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = 16, colour = "#4d4d4d") +
  geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = lab), colour = "white", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.6, y = 0.05, label = "start", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = c(0.1, 2.9, 5.95, 2.9), y = c(0.75, 1.75, 1.8, 0.85),
           label = c("1. Type 0", "2. Type 2", "3. Type 1", "4. Type 3"), size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Type 0" = "#2a78d6", "Type 1" = "#eb6834",
                                 "Type 2" = "#1baf7a", "Type 3" = "#e87ba4"), guide = "none")
```

| Phase  | Meaning                                                              | Usual terms (approximate)                        |
|--------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| ARP    | Area-restricted phase                                                | home range, transient residence, settlement      |
| Type 0 | Unanchored movement, before the first ARP                            | natal or post-release exploration                |
| Type 1 | Loop: leaves an ARP and comes back to the same ARP                   | excursion, foray                                 |
| Type 2 | Network expansion: from a known ARP to a new ARP                     | dispersal, transition to a new residence         |
| Type 3 | Internal transit: between two previously visited ARPs                | return or movement between known residences; migration      |

The equivalences in the last column are approximate. For example, a Type 2
movement may end in a transient residence that the animal later abandons.
Whether an ARP is a home range or a temporary stop depends on how long it lasts
and on the questions of the study, which is why the duration criteria are
arguments of the functions.

This vignette has two parts. **Part I** goes through the workflow with a
simulated data set. **Part II** shows how the main arguments change the
classification, and why.

# Part I. The workflow

## The example data

`sim_tracks` contains hourly GPS fixes of five simulated individuals, with
timing jitter and about 10% of fixes missing. The animals are active at night
and rest during the day, also while dispersing. Directed movements follow
meandering routes, and some include short stopovers of half a day to a day.
The column `behaviour` stores what each animal was really doing in the
simulation, so we can check the results:

- **M01** settles in an area made of two nearby patches and shuttles between
  them. It then moves to a second area, with a stopover on the way, makes a
  looping excursion, and returns to its first area.
- **F02** settles in one area, stays 2.5 days in a second one, and settles in
  two more, with a stopover before the last one.
- **M03** settles in one area and then makes a long transit, during which the
  collar fails for about two days.
- **F04** has a home range made of two nearby patches and makes two looping
  excursions from it.
- **F05** explores with several stopovers, settles for a few days, leaves
  again, and the tracking ends while it is still moving.

```{r data}
head(sim_tracks)
table(sim_tracks$ID, sim_tracks$behaviour)
```

`draw.track()` draws the tracks, optionally coloured by any column:

```{r map-raw, fig.height = 6}
behaviour_cols <- c(stay = "#4d4d4d", stopover = "#eb6834", travel = "#2a78d6")
draw.track(sim_tracks, colour.col = "behaviour", time.col = "timestamp", km = TRUE,
           palette = behaviour_cols)
```

The fixes are irregular, and M03 has a gap of about two days:

```{r intervals, fig.height = 3}
dt_h <- unlist(tapply(as.numeric(sim_tracks$timestamp), sim_tracks$ID,
                      function(t) diff(sort(t)) / 3600))
summary(dt_h)
ggplot(data.frame(dt = dt_h[dt_h <= 6]), aes(dt)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / 6, boundary = 0, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(x = "Interval between fixes (hours)", y = "Count", title = "Intervals up to 6 hours")
```

## 1. Splitting tracks at monitoring gaps

A continuous-time model would interpolate across the gap of M03 and create
locations that were never observed. `divide.track.by.gap()` splits each track
wherever two consecutive fixes are more than `gap.days` apart. `gap.days` can be
a single value or a named list with one value per individual:

```{r gaps}
split_trk <- divide.track.by.gap(sim_tracks, ids = "ID", time.col = "timestamp",
                                 gap.days = 1)
table(split_trk$id_split)
```

```{r map-gap, fig.height = 4}
draw.track(split_trk, colour.col = "id_split", ids = "M03", time.col = "timestamp",
           km = TRUE, palette = c(M03_1 = "#2a78d6", M03_2 = "#eb6834"))
```

## 2. Regularising the tracks

`resample.ctmm()` fits a continuous-time movement model (Calabrese et al. 2016)
to each track and predicts locations every `tint` seconds. Using `id_split` as
identifier resamples each segment separately, so nothing is predicted inside
the gap. `static.cols` copies individual attributes to the output, and the
output coordinates must be in metres:

```{r resample, eval = FALSE}
reg <- resample.ctmm(as.data.frame(split_trk), tint = 3600, ids = "id_split",
                     timestamp = "timestamp", proj.in = 25830,
                     static.cols = "sex", verbose = FALSE)
```

Fitting the models takes a few minutes. Their result, together with the HMM
states of the next step, is stored in `sim_states`:

```{r states}
head(sim_states)
```

## 3. Behavioural states

`fitHMM.wrap()` fits an HMM with gamma step lengths and wrapped Cauchy turning
angles. State 1 is *Transit* and state 2 is *Encamped*. Because our animals rest
every day, we add a third, *stationary* state (`stationary = TRUE`), which is
merged into the encamped state after fitting. Part II shows what happens
without it.

The model is fitted by segment (`id_split`), so that no step crosses the gap of
M03. `fitHMM.wrap()` returns the identifier in a column named `ID`, which here
holds the segment:

```{r hmm, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
reg <- sim_states[, c("id_split", "time", "x", "y", "sex")]

hmm <- fitHMM.wrap(reg, ids = "id_split", stationary = TRUE,
                   mean.step.1 = 700, sd.step.1 = 400,
                   mean.step.2 = 150, sd.step.2 = 100,
                   ang.con.1 = 0.7, ang.con.2 = 0.1)
```

```{r hmm-print}
hmm$models$global_model$mle$step
```

To continue by individual, the segment number is removed from `ID`:

```{r map-states, fig.height = 6}
st <- hmm$data
st$id_split <- as.character(st$ID)
st$ID <- sub("_[0-9]+$", "", st$id_split)
st$state_name <- ifelse(st$state == 1, "Transit", "Encamped")
draw.track(st, colour.col = "state_name", km = TRUE,
           palette = c(Transit = "#eb6834", Encamped = "#2a78d6"))
```

The model can also be fitted to each individual or segment
(`mode = "individual"`) or to groups defined by a column (`mode = "groups"`).

## 4. Area-restricted phases

DBSCAN groups locations that are closer than a distance `epsilon`.
`get.epsilon()` estimates it from the step lengths. By default it is the step
length at which the densities of the two states intersect:

```{r epsilon, message = FALSE}
eps <- get.epsilon(sim_states)
eps
draw.step.densities(sim_states, threshold = eps)
```

`get.arp()` runs DBSCAN on each individual and keeps as ARPs the clusters that
last at least `delta.days` (from their first to their last location) and have
less than `pct.state1` of their locations in the transit state:

```{r arp}
arp <- get.arp(sim_states, epsilon = eps, delta.days = 2, pct.state1 = 0.2)
arp
arp$arp_clusters$F02
```

```{r map-arp, fig.height = 6}
ad <- arp$data
ad$cluster <- ifelse(ad$arp, paste("ARP", ad$cluster_id), "not ARP")
arp_ids <- sort(unique(ad$cluster_id[ad$arp]))
cl_cols <- c("not ARP" = "grey80",
             setNames(rep(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#6250d6", "#e87ba4"),
                          length.out = length(arp_ids)), paste("ARP", arp_ids)))
draw.track(ad, colour.col = "cluster", km = TRUE, palette = cl_cols) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Daytime rests and stopovers during the movements also form small clusters of
encamped locations, but they last less than `delta.days` and are not ARPs.

## 5. Linking ARP clusters

M01 and F04 move back and forth between two nearby patches, and DBSCAN finds
each patch as a separate cluster. Without linking, every trip between them
would be a separate movement. `link.arp()` joins ARP blocks separated by less
than `thres` seconds. The locations in between are flagged as `arp_link`, and
the linked clusters share a `linked_clusters` identifier:

```{r link}
linked <- link.arp(arp, thres = 24 * 3600)
table(linked$data$ID, linked$data$arp_link)
```

`draw.linked.clusters()` shows each ARP cluster as a convex hull, the links as
lines and the linking locations as stars. It returns a `ggplot` object, so it
can be zoomed in like any other plot:

```{r linked-f04, fig.height = 4.5}
draw.linked.clusters(linked, ids = "F04", grid_spacing = 1000)
```

```{r linked-m01, fig.height = 4.5}
m01_arp <- linked$data[linked$data$ID == "M01" & linked$data$linked_clusters == "arp_1", ]
draw.linked.clusters(linked, ids = "M01", grid_spacing = 1000) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(m01_arp$x) + c(-500, 500),
                  ylim = range(m01_arp$y) + c(-500, 500))
```

## 6. Movement phases

```{r classify}
mov <- class.mov(linked)
mov
```

The phases recover the simulated behaviour. M01 expands its network to a second
area (Type 2), makes a loop (Type 1) and returns to its first area (Type 3).
F04 makes two loops from its home range, and the tracking of F05 ends during a
movement whose destination is unknown (`"Type 2 or Type 1"`):

```{r map-phases, fig.height = 6}
draw.track(mov, colour.col = "phase", km = TRUE)
```

```{r map-phases-zoom, fig.height = 4.5}
draw.track(mov, colour.col = "phase", ids = "M01", colour.path = TRUE, km = TRUE)
draw.track(mov, colour.col = "phase", ids = "F05", colour.path = TRUE, km = TRUE)
```

`draw.timeline()` shows the phases along time. Gaps in the monitoring are left
empty:

```{r timeline, fig.height = 3}
draw.timeline(mov)
```

`phase.summary()` turns the classification into a table with one row per
phase, ready for further analysis:

```{r summary}
ph <- phase.summary(mov)
head(ph[, c("ID", "phase", "from", "to", "start", "duration_days", "distance_km")], 8)

# Distance travelled outside ARPs and time until the first ARP
data.frame(
  non_arp_km = round(tapply(ph$distance_km[ph$phase != "ARP"],
                            ph$ID[ph$phase != "ARP"], sum), 1),
  days_to_first_arp = round(tapply(ph$duration_days[ph$phase == "Type 0"],
                                   ph$ID[ph$phase == "Type 0"], sum), 1)
)
```

## 7. Transferring the classification

`transfer.disperseR()` copies the classification to another data set, such as
the original fixes, by matching each row with a location of the `disperseR`
object. `max.diff` (seconds) leaves rows without a close match as `NA`:

```{r transfer, message = FALSE}
raw_phases <- transfer.disperseR(sim_tracks, mov, id.col = "ID",
                                 time.col = "timestamp", max.diff = 3600)
table(raw_phases$ID, raw_phases$phase)
```

# Part II. How choices change the classification

The classification depends on the arguments, and the right values depend on the
species, the sampling interval and the question. This part shows the effect of
the main choices on the same data.

To compare the results with what really happened, we copy the simulated
behaviour to the regular locations (nearest fix in time):

```{r truth}
truth_of <- function(d) {
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(d)), function(i) {
    raw <- sim_tracks[sim_tracks$ID == d$ID[i], ]
    raw$behaviour[which.min(abs(as.numeric(raw$timestamp) - d$time_s[i]))]
  }, character(1))
}
truth <- truth_of(mov$data)

phase_sequence <- function(m) {
  sapply(split(m$data$phase, m$data$ID), function(p) paste(rle(p)$values, collapse = " > "))
}
n_clusters <- function(a) sapply(a$arp_clusters, nrow)
```

## HMM states are not movement phases

A common shortcut is to treat runs of encamped HMM states as residences. The
encamped state, however, includes every daytime rest and every stopover. Here
we compare three views of the same locations: the simulated behaviour, the HMM
state and the `disperseR` phase:

```{r hmm-vs-phases}
resident <- data.frame(
  truth = truth == "stay",
  hmm = mov$data$state == 2,
  disperseR = mov$data$phase == "ARP"
)
# Proportion of the locations of each simulated behaviour classified as resident
round(sapply(resident[, -1], function(r) tapply(r, truth, mean)), 2)

# Number of resident episodes per individual
n_runs <- function(r, id) tapply(r, id, function(z) sum(rle(z)$values))
cbind(truth = n_runs(resident$truth, mov$data$ID),
      hmm = n_runs(resident$hmm, mov$data$ID),
      disperseR = n_runs(resident$disperseR, mov$data$ID))
```

The HMM labels much of the time spent travelling as encamped (the daily rests
and the stopovers) and splits each dispersal into many short "residences".
`disperseR` keeps the stopovers and rests inside the movements:

```{r hmm-vs-phases-plot, fig.height = 2.6}
cmp <- rbind(
  data.frame(ID = "1. simulated", time = mov$data$time, status = truth),
  data.frame(ID = "2. HMM state", time = mov$data$time,
             status = ifelse(resident$hmm, "stay", "travel")),
  data.frame(ID = "3. disperseR", time = mov$data$time,
             status = ifelse(resident$disperseR, "stay", "travel"))
)
cmp <- cmp[rep(mov$data$ID, 3) == "F05", ]
draw.timeline(cmp, phase.col = "status", palette = behaviour_cols) +
  labs(title = "F05: resident (stay) or not")
```

## Activity modes or movement modes: the HMM states

What the HMM states capture depends on the number of states and on the
starting values. A two-state model started near resting and moving values
separates *activity modes*: daytime rests on one side, and every movement,
including the movements inside home ranges, on the other:

```{r hmm-2states, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
hmm2 <- fitHMM.wrap(reg, ids = "id_split",
                    mean.step.1 = 300, sd.step.1 = 300,
                    mean.step.2 = 20, sd.step.2 = 20,
                    ang.con.1 = 0.5, ang.con.2 = 0.1)
st2 <- hmm2$data
st2$ID <- sub("_[0-9]+$", "", as.character(st2$ID))
```

```{r hmm-2states-compare, message = FALSE}
hmm2$models$global_model$mle$step
eps2 <- get.epsilon(st2)
c(three_states = eps, two_states = eps2)
```

The step-length densities now cross at a few tens of metres, and DBSCAN with
that `epsilon` only groups the locations of each resting site. The ARPs break
into many small clusters and the classification fills with spurious loops:

```{r hmm-2states-arp}
arp2 <- get.arp(st2, epsilon = eps2, delta.days = 2, pct.state1 = 0.5)
rbind(three_states = n_clusters(arp),
      two_states = n_clusters(arp2))
phase_sequence(class.mov(link.arp(arp2, thres = 24 * 3600)))[c("M01", "F02")]
```

The three-state model, in contrast, keeps the movements inside the ARPs in the
encamped state, so the encamped locations describe the space used during each
phase. Inspecting the estimated step lengths of each state helps to decide how
many states the model needs and what they mean (Pohle et al. 2017).

## The distance threshold epsilon

`get.epsilon()` offers three methods (`"density"`, `"mean"` and `"median"`)
that can be applied to all data, per individual or per group:

```{r epsilon-table, message = FALSE}
eps_tab <- sapply(c("density", "mean", "median"), function(m) {
  c(global = get.epsilon(sim_states, method = m),
    unlist(get.epsilon(sim_states, method = m, mode = "individual", ids = "ID")),
    unlist(get.epsilon(sim_states, method = m, mode = "groups", group.col = "sex")))
})
round(eps_tab)
```

A smaller `epsilon` splits an area into more clusters, and a larger one merges
nearby areas or joins stopovers to the route:

```{r epsilon-effect}
eps_values <- c(eps / 4, eps / 2, eps, 2 * eps, 4 * eps)
eps_effect <- sapply(eps_values, function(e)
  n_clusters(get.arp(sim_states, epsilon = e, delta.days = 2, pct.state1 = 0.2)))
colnames(eps_effect) <- paste0(round(eps_values), " m")
eps_effect
```

## Duration, activity and minimum points

`delta.days` decides how long a cluster must last to be an ARP. It is measured
from the first to the last location of the cluster, so patches visited
repeatedly last longer than each single visit. The stay of 2.5 days of F02 is
an ARP with `delta.days = 2` but not with `delta.days = 3`. A lenient
`pct.state1` accepts clusters at the border of the areas that include transit
locations. `minPts` decides which locations are core points of a cluster: a
larger value can split loosely connected areas, such as the patches of M01:

```{r arp-variants}
n_arp <- function(delta = 2, pct = 0.2, minPts = 3) {
  n_clusters(get.arp(sim_states, epsilon = eps, delta.days = delta,
                     pct.state1 = pct, minPts = minPts))
}
rbind("delta.days = 0.5" = n_arp(delta = 0.5),
      "delta.days = 1"   = n_arp(delta = 1),
      "delta.days = 2"   = n_arp(delta = 2),
      "delta.days = 3"   = n_arp(delta = 3),
      "pct.state1 = 0.5" = n_arp(pct = 0.5),
      "minPts = 10"      = n_arp(minPts = 10))
```

With a short `delta.days`, stopovers become ARPs and the movements are cut into
pieces. The proportion of stopover locations classified as ARP:

```{r arp-short}
mov_short <- class.mov(link.arp(get.arp(sim_states, epsilon = eps, delta.days = 0.5,
                                        pct.state1 = 0.2), thres = 24 * 3600))
rbind("delta.days = 0.5" = tapply(mov_short$data$phase[truth == "stopover"] == "ARP",
                                  mov_short$data$ID[truth == "stopover"], mean),
      "delta.days = 2"   = tapply(mov$data$phase[truth == "stopover"] == "ARP",
                                  mov$data$ID[truth == "stopover"], mean))
```

## Linking threshold

`thres` decides which short trips out of an ARP are links and which are
movements. The number of Type 1 and Type 3 movements drops quickly as `thres`
grows, until it reaches the duration of the shuttles between patches. It then
stays stable while `thres` is shorter than the loops and the movements between
areas:

```{r thres-curve, fig.height = 3.5, warning = FALSE}
thres_h <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96)
counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(thres_h, function(h) {
  p <- phase.summary(suppressWarnings(class.mov(link.arp(arp, thres = h * 3600))))
  data.frame(thres = h, phase = c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3"),
             n = as.vector(table(factor(p$phase, c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3")))))
}))
ggplot(counts, aes(thres, n, colour = phase)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 24, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Type 1" = "#eb6834", "Type 2" = "#1baf7a",
                                 "Type 3" = "#e87ba4"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 12, 24, 48, 72, 96)) +
  labs(x = "thres (hours)", y = "Number of movements (all individuals)")
```

Without linking (`thres = 0`), every shuttle between the two patches of M01 and
F04 becomes a movement. With a very long `thres`, the loops, and even the
movement of M01 between its two areas, are absorbed into the ARPs:

```{r thres-sequences}
thres_seq <- sapply(c(0, 24, 96), function(h)
  phase_sequence(suppressWarnings(class.mov(link.arp(arp, thres = h * 3600))))[c("M01", "F04")])
colnames(thres_seq) <- paste("thres =", c(0, 24, 96), "h")
thres_seq
```

## Establishment

With `establish = TRUE`, an ARP only counts as an established site if the
individual stays there at least `establish.days`. Shorter stays become part of
the movement. The duration is measured over the whole stay in a linked ARP, so
M01, which rarely stays three days in a row in one of its patches, still
establishes its first area:

```{r establish}
est_seq <- sapply(c(1, 3, 9), function(d)
  phase_sequence(class.mov(linked, establish = TRUE,
                           establish.days = d))[c("F02", "M01", "F05")])
colnames(est_seq) <- paste("establish.days =", c(1, 3, 9))
est_seq
```

With `establish.days = 3`, the 2.5-day stay of F02 becomes part of a single
Type 2 movement. With `establish.days = 9`, only the longest settlements count:
the 6-day settlement of F05 is not established, so its whole track is an
unanchored movement (Type 0).

## Minimum convex polygon for links

With `arp.links = "mcp"`, linking locations stay in the ARP only if they fall
inside the minimum convex polygon of the preceding ARP cluster. Otherwise they
become loops (Type 1). Trips between two separate patches fall outside the
polygon:

```{r mcp}
phase_sequence(class.mov(linked, arp.links = "mcp"))[c("M01", "F04")]
```

## Transferring to the raw fixes

The matching method of `transfer.disperseR()` matters at the transitions
between phases. `"temporal"` takes the nearest location in time; `"forward"`
and `"backward"` the nearest later or earlier one; `"spatial"` the nearest in
space, which may be far in time; and `"movement"` and `"arp"` give priority to
the movement or to the ARP phase when a fix falls between both:

```{r transfer-methods, message = FALSE}
methods <- c("temporal", "spatial", "forward", "backward", "movement", "arp")
tr <- lapply(setNames(methods, methods), function(m)
  transfer.disperseR(sim_tracks, mov, id.col = "ID", time.col = "timestamp",
                     method = m, max.diff = 3600))
data.frame(
  agreement_with_temporal = round(sapply(tr, function(d)
    mean(d$phase == tr$temporal$phase, na.rm = TRUE)), 3),
  fixes_in_ARP = sapply(tr, function(d) sum(d$phase == "ARP", na.rm = TRUE)),
  no_match_within_1h = sapply(tr, function(d) sum(is.na(d$phase))))
```

## Practical recommendations

- Express `delta.days`, `establish.days` and `thres` in terms of the biology of
  the species: how long a settlement must last to be meaningful, and how long a
  trip between nearby patches usually takes.
- `epsilon`, `minPts` and the HMM states depend on the sampling interval. With
  4-hour fixes, for example, steps are longer and there are fewer locations per
  day than in this hourly example.
- Check the HMM states and the clusters on maps (`draw.track()`) before
  classifying the movements, and compare a few values of each argument, as in
  this part, to see how robust the classification is.
